messages.author: 839dfa09184985a5
messages.subject: Testing Distributions
parts:
I noticed that in the distribution testing framework, cdfs (and now
cdf_log and ccdf_log) test the lower bound/upper bound of the random
variable, y, but log prob doesn't. Is there a reason for this?


Peter

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Testing Distributions
parts:
On Jun 28, 2013, at 11:50 AM, Peter Li wrote:
> I noticed that in the distribution testing framework, cdfs (and now cdf_log and ccdf_log) test the lower bound/upper bound of the random variable, y, but log prob doesn't. Is there a reason for this?

Yes, I couldn't reason around what we consider upper and lower bounds. If we take the normal_log(y, mu, sigma) as an example, we can push in {-inf, +inf} for y and mu and expect the result to be -Inf (well -- off by constants, I guess), but what about sigma? If we push in sigma = {0, Inf} do we expect -Inf? Does this hold in general? How do we encode in the tests the lower and upper bounds for every parameter? (I guess I did it for the cdf's, so maybe it's not that difficult.)

We could always test just the first argument, y.

Feel free to change the tests. I built them a while ago and haven't really gone back to update them.


Daniel

messages.author: 839dfa09184985a5
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Testing Distributions
parts:
I thought the upper/lower bound tests were only for the first argument
regardless, especially since it only takes in one lower bound (in the
cdf tests). If the lower bound were assigned to all the params, I think
errors would be thrown, since in the case of the normal distribution,
the lower bound of y is negative infinity (so has_lower_bound() returns
false) but sigma has a lower bound of 0.0, so an error would be thrown
if we tried to pass in negative infty for sigma.


Peter

There was some discussion around the behavior that CDFs should
have outside of their support. I would prefer to check the
arguments to CDFs just like the probability functions and have
the same configurable behavior.

For example, uniform(L,U) has support in [L,U] so in
unfirom_log(y,L,U) a check is made that y is in [L,U] and
if not, an exception is raised (or -infinity or NaN returned depending
on config). I'd like to do the same thing with uniform_cdf(y,L,U).
